title: Connection Shepherd and Ephemeral Eviction Gateway
author: Maya Chen
release_notes: Introduces a Connection Shepherd service and an Ephemeral Eviction Gateway that enable staged connection fencing and SLO-aware soft-evacuations. Improves tenant-level fairness during regional overloads and reduces tail-latency spikes during drains. Backported hotfix to release-2025.10.
description:
Context and motivation: During a recent incident we observed connection storms when nodes were being drained for maintenance or when transient network partitions caused large cohorts of long-running connections to re-originate to the same nodes. Existing soft-eviction logic uses token-bucket based shedding at request-level which reduces throughput but does not give fine-grained control over active socket lifetimes or connection-local sequencing. This led to tail latency amplification and SLO violations for high-priority tenants.

Goal: Add a Connection Shepherd component and an Ephemeral Eviction Gateway to coordinate staged connection fencing, graceful connection leash expiration, and SLO-aware partial evacuations so that: 1) long-lived connections are drained in a controlled, tenant-aware order, 2) transient overloads can be mitigated with minimal impact to P99 latency for priority traffic, and 3) regional failover events produce a predictable, bounded surge instead of a spike.

What this PR does (summary):
- Introduces connection-shepherd/ service: an in-cluster controller that keeps per-node connection catalogs and computes staged fence windows using tenant SLO profiles, recent traffic histograms, and KV-cache pressure signals.
- Adds ephemeral-eviction-gateway: an L7 shim that applies connection fences at the proxy layer, implements soft-eviction (TCP/TLS polite windowed FIN/GOAWAY where applicable), and exposes a graceful-drain API for orchestration.
- Implements a connection leash mechanism: when a node is marked for drain, existing connections receive a leash TTL so non-critical sockets can be preemptively wound down while critical tenant flows get extended leases.
- Tenant prioritization policy: leverages existing tenant priority buckets and extends them with an emergency-shed weight and preservation budget. Policies are configurable via the existing operator CRD (ConnectionFenceSpec).
- Flow-control watermarking: introduces a new metric (conn_surge_watermark) used by the autoscaler and SLO enforcer to trigger preemptive soft-evictions before token-bucket based request-level shedding engages.
- Metrics/telemetry: per-tenant drain timelines, leash expirations, partial-eviction counts, and region-coalesce statistics wired into Console dashboards and tracing.
- Backport: a small hotfix was applied to release-2025.10 to address an edge-case where leash TTLs were not honored for HTTP/2 GOAWAY; that change is included as a cherry-pick.

Files changed (high level):
- connection-shepherd/ controller: several new files (controller.go, scheduler.go, policy.go, lease_store.go) and unit tests.
- ephemeral-eviction-gateway/ proxy shim: main gateway implementation, graceful-drain handlers, HTTP/2 GOAWAY support and tests.
- operator/ crd: ConnectionFenceSpec CRD additions and validation webhooks.
- console/ telemetry: dashboard JSON, new metrics exporter instrumentation.
- docs/ runbooks: new runbook 'connection-drain-and-surge-mitigation.md' and operator guide snippets.

Commits: (high level)
- feat(conn-shepherd): initial controller scaffold and lease store (3 commits)
- feat(eviction-gateway): graceful-drain API and hut-run proxy shim (2 commits)
- perf(shepherd): tenant scoring and staged window algorithm (1 commit)
- test: unit/integration tests for GOAWAY and leash expiry (2 commits)
- ci: add e2e test job that runs drain scenarios in perf-lab (1 commit)
- hotfix: cherry-pick GOAWAY TTL fix to release-2025.10 (1 commit)

Design notes and rationale:
- We purposely separate connection-level control from request-level shedding to avoid double-accounting and to preserve in-flight work for high-priority flows. The shepherd computes an evacuation plan (ordered windows) and ships leash TTLs; the eviction gateway enforces the plan in-proxy.
- Leash TTLs are advisory for non-critical connections (enforced with polite close) and mandatory for lower-priority tenant flows if a hard drain is requested. This duality allows operators to do gradual soft-evacuations with fallthrough hard-drain if a node doesn't decommission timely.
- The conn_surge_watermark is keyed on both active connection count and recent per-tenant token consumption; it allows the autoscaler to pre-scale and the SLO enforcer to nudge the shepherd into more aggressive staging.

Testing and CI:
- Unit tests cover scheduler heuristics, lease expiry, and the HTTP/2 GOAWAY path.
- Integration e2e runs in the benchmark-lab simulate rolling drains with mixed tenant traffic (embedding-heavy, chat streaming, short-lived API calls).
- CI initially failed (flaky GOAWAY race flagged by integration job). I reproduced locally, added an additional synchronization barrier and a deterministic retry in the gateway; reran CI and all checks passed.

Review conversation (highlights):
- Carlos: "Nice separation of concerns. Please add more comments around the staged window heuristic and include a simple example in the CRD docs."
- Maya: "Added detailed comments and an example stanza in operator docs; also added a unit test for the heuristic edge-case."
- Anika: "Can we avoid introducing a second global controller? Can the shepherd be sharded?"
- Maya: "Yes — implemented a sharding token so the shepherd can horizontalize; updated controller.go and added sharding tests. The default remains single-shard for small clusters."
- Liam: "Metric cardinality looks high; ensure we aggregate per-tenant buckets to avoid cardinality explosion."
- Maya: "Adjusted exporter to rollup low-traffic tenants and added sampling for the 'drain-timeline' trace spans."

Backward compatibility and operator impact:
- CRD changes are additive and validated; existing operator configs will continue to work.
- There is an operator upgrade step to enable the default lease TTLs; operators can keep the feature off by setting ConnectionFenceSpec.enabled=false.

Operational playbook (short):
- To trigger a soft-evacuation: kubectl annotate node redwood/node-5 redwood.io/drain=soft and set operator ConnectionFenceSpec.enabled=true. Console will surface the evacuation plan and leash expirations.
- If leash TTLs are not honored by a tenant, the gateway supports escalating to forced closure after a configurable grace period.

Risks and mitigations:
- Risk: metric cardinality growth — mitigated by aggregation and sampling changes.
- Risk: under-evacuation causing long tails — mitigated by fallback hard-drain path and autoscaler integration.

Merge outcome and follow-ups:
- Merged via squash after two approvals (Carlos, Anika) and green CI on main and release-2025.10 backport pipeline.
- Follow-ups filed: ENG-9012 (observability: add drift detection between planner and gateway), ENG-9013 (test: long-duration soak in perf-lab), SRE-121 (runbook automation to detect leash TTL misses).

Notes on uniqueness: This approach focuses on explicit connection-level orchestration (leashes, staged fences, ephemeral eviction gateway) rather than purely request-level shedder changes. It provides a predictable, tenant-aware partial evacuation mechanism that complements existing SLO enforcers and token-bucket shedder pieces. The PR also includes a targeted hotfix for HTTP/2 GOAWAY behavior which was the immediate cause for the original incident.
